event: During HIL simulation flight 1 of VXE-102 (TIQUILA Windows 11 regression testing), after a second route was uploaded and the first re-uploaded, the GCS and OGCS showed the aircraft flying route Flight while it was actually flying Test Route; no damage (simulation).
component: GCS/OGCS route upload status and active route display
failure_mode: active route shown as the re-uploaded route while the aircraft kept flying the previously uploaded route, which was shown as not uploaded
contributing: route re-uploaded while the aircraft was already flying a different route
found during Windows 11 software regression testing

evidence.quote: After that, the display indicated that the aircraft was flying Flight while it was actually flying Test Route that was shown as not uploaded.
The dashed line indicates the aircraft thinks it’s flying racetrack 3 of the uploaded mission but it’s flying the other racetrack 3
The line from the aircraft shows it as flying a racetrack that is not the uploaded racetrack

would_settle_it.what: GCS map showing which route and loiter the aircraft reports versus the path actually flown
autopilot active route and waypoint number versus GCS uploaded-route state after the re-upload, to tell a GCS display fault from an autopilot reporting fault

reasoning: The ticket only describes the symptom: after re-uploading route Flight, both the GCS and OGCS showed the aircraft on Flight while it flew Test Route. The route files show Flight uses waypoints 2 to 4 and Test Route uses waypoints 5 to 8, so the two routes were distinct. The fault sits in the route upload and active route state between the ground software and the autopilot, but nothing says which side reported wrongly, and the ticket was closed for end of product support.
notes: HIL simulation, not a real flight. Both GCS and OGCS showed the same wrong state, so an autopilot reporting fault cannot be excluded; ground_software is the best reading only. The description mentions racetrack 3 although the route files number the racetracks 4 and 7. Closed without investigation (end of support).

event: During HIL simulation flight 2 of VXE-102 (TIQUILA Windows 11 regression testing), the right aft lift motor did not start at launch and the launch was aborted on low climb rate; no damage (simulation).
failure_mode: lift motor did not start at launch, causing a low climb rate abort
contributing: HIL simulation setup during Windows 11 software regression testing

evidence.quote: During flight #2 the right aft lift motor did not start at launch.
Warnings were received for “Climb abort low climb rate”.
TIQ doing Windows 11 software regression testing.

would_settle_it.what: motor 3 throttle command, ESC status and RPM at launch, to tell whether the motor was never commanded, the ESC did not respond, or the simulator failed it

reasoning: The low climb rate abort worked as designed because one lift motor did not start, so the degraded input is the rear right lift motor. The ticket gives no data on why it did not start, and in a HIL setup it may be simulated, so the evidence stops at the propulsion system for that position.
notes: HIL simulation, not a real flight: it is not stated whether the lift motor and ESC were real hardware or simulated, so propulsion is a best reading and a simulator or software cause is possible. Right aft mapped to motor 3 (rear right). Closed for end of product support with no investigation.

event: The MCM on VXE-918 (Precision) powered on but could not be reached over GbE or serial; the MCM was replaced under RMA-933 and the returned unit was found to hang in its secure boot chain before reaching Linux.
component: MCM (Jetson module boot firmware, OP-TEE trusted application load)
failure_mode: boot hangs in OP-TEE after secure boot authentication (RPC allocation failed, ldelf failed); Linux never starts, no login and no network
contributing: possible hard power cycle during EKS payload writes (team view)
possible firmware partition mismatch
possible overheating when powered without cooling

evidence.quote: E/TC:?? 00 get_rpc_alloc_res:645 RPC allocation failed. Non-secure world result: ret=0xffff0000 ret_origin=0
-- Boot halts here. Linux normal world never reached. No login prompt. Network interfaces unresponsive. --
Unable to gain access through either interface. No ping on either interface. Serial shows activity on boot but does not reach login and does not accept input.
I would concur that we should proceed with a reflash.
R&R MCM component and retain for investigation.

team_root_cause:
Unsure of exact cause cannot be definitely determined since the device history is not completely known. Given that the intake form shows that the device was functional at some point, it seems most likely that a hard power cycle during one of the EKS payload file writes has corrupted the boot flow (the security components check out during auth but when the system actually tries to use them, it crashes and fails to boot up.) A second possibility could be that the system has some kind of firmware component mismatch, but, if the aircraft has flown before this is less likely.   
Notably, though, we

would_settle_it.what: whether a full reflash from one L4T BSP package restores boot; if so it was partition corruption, if not a hardware fault
whether MCM temperatures without active cooling could damage the module

reasoning: The serial capture shows the secure boot chain authenticating and loading, then OP-TEE failing to allocate memory and load a trusted application, after which Linux never starts; that explains the lack of ping and login. This names the failing stage on the MCM directly. Why the boot firmware got into that state (power cycle during EKS writes, firmware mismatch or heat) is not shown, and the reflash that would confirm corruption is recommended but not reported done.
notes: Team Root Cause field is longer than 600 characters and is truncated. The RMA-933 intake PDF has no extractable text. The customer received a replacement MCM board (127-116969-01) under warranty; the failed MCM's reflash outcome is not recorded.

event: VXE-885 (USAACE training) began forward transition at a few feet AGL right after launch because the first launch waypoint had been set to an MSL altitude below ground; the operators aborted and the aircraft settled back to the ground.
component: launch route first waypoint altitude (MSL entry in OGCS)
failure_mode: launch waypoint altitude set to about 4750 ft MSL, 10 ft below the calibration ground altitude, so the transition goal was already met at low height
contributing: OGCS did not block launch transition altitudes below ground (limits added in OGCS 1.3.3)
altitude field editing can leave an unintended value, as shown in the attached video

evidence.quote: it appears the operator changed the first launch waypoint from the default 200ft AGL to a value of ~4750ft MSL, which is 10ft below the MSL value at calibration of 4760ft.
Aircraft got to hover at ~4 ft AGL, initiated forward-transition (airspeed built to 97 fps), then airspeed collapsed in 1 second (~45 fps/s deceleration) and never recovered.
OGCS 1.3.3 implemented limits on allowed launch transition altitudes, and OGCS 1.4.3 implemented limits on allowed landing transition altitudes.
Here is a video of deleting the 3 from 300 and attempting to change it to 2 for 200 but ending up with just 2 .

team_root_cause: Launch route was modified to use an unsafe MSL altitude which was 10ft below the ground.  Unclear why the operator made this change or if it was accidental.
reasoning: The OGCS log review found the first launch waypoint changed from 200 ft AGL to about 4750 ft MSL, 10 ft below the ground reference, so the autopilot saw its climb goal as met and started the transition almost on the ground. Flight data confirm the aircraft hovered at about 4 ft, built airspeed and then settled back. The input came from the operator, and OGCS at the time had no check to stop it.
notes: Operators reported transition at about 20 ft AGL, but the log review puts the aircraft at 2 to 5 ft AGL throughout. Whether the operator change was deliberate or an editing slip is unknown; the later video shows how an edit can leave an unintended value. Corrective action closed with OGCS 1.3.3.

event: VXE-677 (TIQUILA, US exercise) climbed instead of descending in the IP2/3 orbit during recovery and ignored a lower waypoint, so the crew took manual control and commanded Land Immediate at 1 percent main battery; no damage.
component: thermal updraft in the landing pattern
failure_mode: aircraft gained altitude in the IP2/3 orbit and could not descend as commanded
contributing: main battery depleted to 1 percent during the extended orbit
air data pod replaced by the operator, so an air data fault was suspected locally

evidence.quote: it was observed that the aircraft remained in the IP2/3 orbit for an extended period and was increasing in altitude rather than descending as intended.
Despite this, the aircraft maintained its altitude, disregarding the mission update.
Operator needs to not land in a thermal.
DT replacing Air Data Pod  (Not under LM direction)

team_view_in_comments: Operator needs to not land in a thermal.

would_settle_it.what: climb rate, throttle and pitch in the IP2/3 orbit, and air data altitude versus GPS altitude, to confirm updraft versus an air data or guidance fault

reasoning: The only engineering conclusion is a one-line comment that the aircraft was landed in a thermal, which fits an aircraft rising in orbit and not descending to a lower waypoint. No log analysis is attached to support it, and the operator separately replaced the air data pod, so an air data fault remains a credible alternative.
notes: Closed as Won't Do. The AAR archive is listed only and no data plots are in the ticket. The thermal reading rests on a single comment.

event: VXE-1042 (LRR training) auto-aborted a launch on high vibration in winds of 30 to 40 fps; landed without damage and flew twice more without issue.
failure_mode: excess VTOL vibration from high wind tripped the launch abort
contributing: possible prop blade damage raised but not confirmed
intake later found a loose ODU connector collar with no visible thread locker

evidence.quote: It definitely has a good bit more vibe than the one reference log I was able to find from FLOPs for that aircraft.
The winds show 30-40fps which as at/above the limit (30fps ~= 20mph).
closing this ticket the aircraft has flown 2 more times no issues.
Collar on ODU conmedor t conneds to wiratip loose. No lockte Visibe.

team_root_cause: Winds out of limitations causing excessive vibration causing the aborted launch.

would_settle_it.what: vibration level of the aborted launch compared with the reference log
Eric Brewer's vibration and wind plots for this launch

reasoning: The abort was triggered by vibration well above the reference log, and the log showed winds of 30 to 40 fps, at or above the limit, which is known to raise VTOL vibration. Physical inspection found nothing and the aircraft flew twice more without an abort, which supports wind over a hardware cause. This is a designed abort on a degraded input, so it is scored as narrowed to environment.
notes: The intake form (added a month later, OCR text badly garbled) notes a loose ODU connector collar on a lift boom or wing tip connector with no thread locker visible; its link to the vibration is not discussed.

event: VXE-930 (MOLSON) twice showed main battery low and started an RTB during a mission, then the battery reading recovered and it resumed; operators also reported it broke orbit and ignored commands, and landed early.
component: main battery to avionics power chain (main battery, current sensor, avionics box or harness)
failure_mode: intermittent low main battery reading triggering RTB, then recovering
contributing: many low packet percentage events in the log
radio found misconfigured with settings profile missing at SCO, suspected customer FIPS reset
high winds (groundspeed up to 90 fps)

evidence.quote: While on its mission it showed that the main battery was low and commenced a RTB, during the RTB the battery life with back to its normal percentage and returned to the mission.
This flight flew an orbit until a GoTO to IP1 was received. At which point it recovered as expected.
In any case I agree it seemed like it tracked the orbit ok so I’m not sure what erratic behavior was observed.
Main battery voltage drops with fwd motor throttle. Suggests intermittent or high resistance connection in the main battery, current sensor, avbox, or harness from main battery to avionics box.
Looked into by SCO- Radio seems to have been misconfigured, and the settings profile is missing. Suspected FIPS reset done by customer

team_view_in_comments: Waiting on separate 930 investigation data to resolve, believed voltage issue is causing behavior. Probable cause Battery.

would_settle_it.what: main battery voltage and current at each low battery RTB, and link packet loss around the reported lost commands

would_settle_it.file: physical_inspection of main battery, current sensor and avionics box harness
would_settle_it.what: high resistance or intermittent connection in the main battery to avionics power chain, as suspected in VXEP-1557

attachments_read: 54234_CF-855-001 Return Material Authorization (RMA) Request Form - 820_930_929_fuel cell.pdf.md
reasoning: The RTBs were the designed response to a main battery low reading that came and went, which matches the earlier VXEP-1557 finding on the same aircraft of main battery voltage dropping with throttle through a suspected intermittent or high resistance connection. Log review found the orbit and recovery normal, so the broken orbit claim is not supported. The cause is narrowed to the main battery power chain, not to one part.
notes: The correct dataset was not confirmed until August 2026. The lost-commands report may relate to the radio misconfiguration found at SCO (RMA-972) or to low packet percentage, but nothing ties them. Battery chosen following VXEP-1557 and the team executive summary; harness is equally possible. The 930 intake PDF has no extractable text.

event: VXE-884 (USAACE) drifted and made an uncommanded 90 degree turn during VTOL descent to land, then pitched down from about 10 ft AGL and crashed, separating the center wing.
failure_mode: loss of thrust on the front left lift motor (command saturated high as the aircraft pitched down and rolled left); bench test showed the motor does not home correctly
contributing: brass ballast weight on the VTOL board stack found hanging with broken nylon screws, possibly disturbing the MPU 9250 IMU
low energy warnings after impact
loss of GPS lock after impact

evidence.quote: Left front command goes high at the same time it pitches down and rolls left.
i removed the left front motor and brought it to electronics and found that the motor does not home correctly.
The center wing panel was opened and one of the brass ballast weights on the VTOL board stack was found to be hanging as shown below.
Or had it previously broken off which then caused the MPU 9250 to miscalculate acceleration?
Failure not reproducible in SLO.  Nevertheless, root cause is likely Left Front Motor.

team_view_in_comments: Failure not reproducible in SLO.  Nevertheless, root cause is likely Left Front Motor.

would_settle_it.what: motor 1 throttle command saturating against attitude at the pitch down, and whether the other motors respond normally
VXE 884 Investigation.pptx findings on the left front motor
run the left front motor and ESC under load and open the ESC to tell motor from ESC fault, and check whether the homing fault is crash damage
IMU acceleration and attitude before the drift and turn, to test whether the loose ballast weight disturbed the MPU 9250

attachments_read: 57714_AV 884(part 2) CF-855-001 Return Material Authorization (RMA) Request Form(part2).pdf.md
reasoning: The log shows the front left lift motor command going high as the aircraft pitched down and rolled left, which is the signature of that motor not delivering thrust, and the removed motor later failed to home correctly on the bench. But the failure did not reproduce, the homing fault may be crash damage, and the last finding was a loose ballast weight on the VTOL board stack that could have upset the IMU, which the investigator himself left as an open question. So the evidence narrows to the front left motor or ESC, with an IMU disturbance as a credible alternative.
notes: No Root Cause field; the team view is from the Issue Status field. Left front mapped to motor 1 (front left). The drift and 90 degree turn earlier in the descent are not explained by any analysis in the ticket. The two 884 intake PDFs are identical and their OCR is badly garbled. VXEP-628 lists this ticket as Investigating.
